task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper explainer for general readers answering the question: What makes connecting offshore wind farms to the electric grid so difficult, and why does it matter for clean energy? Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of May 28, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: Offshore wind farms generate electricity miles from shore; getting that power to land requires undersea cables, offshore substations, and onshore grid upgrades that can cost as much as the turbines themselves.
High-voltage direct current (HVDC) cables are used for long undersea runs because they lose less energy than alternating current (AC) over distances greater than about 60 kilometers.
At each end of an HVDC cable, converter stations transform DC to AC for the onshore grid or AC to DC from the offshore turbines; each station costs hundreds of millions of dollars.

Connecting a large wind farm to the onshore grid requires upgrading or building onshore transmission lines from the cable landing point to where the power can be used; this may require crossing populated areas and acquiring rights-of-way.
Permitting onshore transmission lines is often slower than building the offshore project; in some cases, transmission delays have caused wind farms to wait years before delivering full power.

Grid integration engineer Dr. Lena Korhonen of Atlantic Grid Institute said: "The hardest part is not the cable. It is convincing communities, regulators, and grid operators across multiple jurisdictions to agree on who pays for what and where the cables come ashore."

Offshore wind output varies with wind conditions; the grid must accommodate this variability, either through storage, backup generation, or interconnection with larger areas where wind is available when it is calm locally.

The capacity factor of offshore wind — the percentage of time it operates at or near full output — averages 40 to 55%; this is higher than onshore wind but still less than around-the-clock sources like nuclear.

Grid codes — technical standards defining how generation must connect to the grid — require offshore wind to provide fault ride-through (staying connected during grid disturbances) and reactive power support; meeting these requires inverter technology that adds cost.

In countries with many offshore projects, shared offshore grid infrastructure — a meshed offshore grid connecting multiple farms before bringing power ashore — can reduce the number of cable landings needed.
Offshore cable installation requires specialized vessels; demand for these vessels has exceeded supply as offshore wind development accelerated globally.
Onshore grid substations near coastal landing points are often built for existing load and must be upgraded or new ones built to accept large blocks of offshore generation.
Dr. Korhonen said the interconnection queue — the list of projects waiting for grid studies to determine how they connect — is a major bottleneck in the U.S., with multi-year waits common.

The Jones Act requires ships operating between U.S. ports to be U.S.-built, -owned, and -crewed; its application to offshore wind installation vessels is ambiguous and has complicated the use of European-built specialized vessels in U.S. waters.

A meshed North Sea offshore grid is under development by several European countries to share wind resources across national grids; it involves international agreements on capacity allocation and cost sharing.
The cost of undersea cables has increased due to copper and steel price rises and high demand; some offshore projects have been delayed or cancelled partly because of cable procurement challenges.

Floating offshore wind — turbines mounted on floating platforms rather than fixed to the seabed — extends wind development into deeper water but requires dynamic cables that can flex with platform movement, adding complexity.

Dr. Korhonen said the U.S. Northeast coast faces a particular challenge: multiple states have separate procurement programs, creating fragmented demand that makes planning regional grid infrastructure difficult.

Long-distance HVDC transmission can also connect offshore wind in the U.S. South to demand centers in the Northeast, supplementing local offshore development; such projects require crossing multiple states' regulatory jurisdictions.
Offshore substations must be maintained by personnel in all weather conditions; helicopter access is restricted in high winds, creating maintenance windows that affect availability.
